title: MODIFYING CLASSROOM ACOUSTICAL ENVIRONMENT TO AFFECT SENSORY BEHAVIOURS AND LEARNING OF CHILDREN WITH ASD
research_question:
Stage 1 Study: Is there a direct impact of the classroom environment's sensory stressor architectural elements upon the triggering behaviours of the participating children with ASD and restrictive input inhibiting their On-task learning?
Stage 2 Study: Is there a direct ramification of the Independent Variable (IV) RT 60, and the LAeq and LA90 correlates upon delineated sensory behaviours in children with ASD?
Stage 3 Study: Is there a direct impact of the Independent Variable (IV) RT60 and the LAeq and LA90 correlates upon 1:1 ratio on-task sustained performativity targeted behaviour in children with ASD?

participants.description: Four male students aged 9 to 11 years with a medical diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) from Oasis School for Autism in Lahore, Pakistan. Socioeconomic background was mixed (upper, middle, lower-class strata). Linguistic and communicational disorders ranged from impaired speech to non-verbal.
participants.recruitment: Purposive sampling from Oasis School for Autism.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Classroom environment before acoustic modification, characterized by long reverberation time (Tmf 1.11s) and higher noise levels (LAeq 75.8 dBA during group activity).

Classroom environment after acoustic modification, achieved by installing sound-absorbent wall panels (50mm thick yellow-coloured fibreglass wool sheet with silver backing, light blue cloth cover) to reduce reverberation time (Tmf 0.39s) and noise levels (LAeq 64.08 dBA during group activity).

findings.antecedent: Classroom environment's sensory stressor architectural elements (noise/acoustics, light, spatial layout, temperature, smell)
findings.consequent: Triggering behaviours and inhibition of on-task learning in children with ASD
findings.mechanism: Expert interviews validated noise/acoustics as a significant environmental independent variable affecting children's heterogeneous, idiosyncratic, and subjective behaviours.
findings.quote: The examination identified noise/ acoustics as the significant environmental independent variable

findings.antecedent: Noise (auditory sensitivity)
findings.consequent: Disruptive behaviours in children with ASD
findings.mechanism: More than half of interviewees (7 out of 9) mentioned noise reflecting auditory sensitivity as a dominant feature triggering disruptive behaviours.
findings.quote: More than half of the interviewee participants (7 out of 9) mentioned noise reflecting auditory sensitivity as a dominant feature triggering disruptive behaviours

findings.antecedent: Ambient noise (clutter of chairs, furniture shuffle, children’s screams, classroom children’s noise)
findings.consequent: On-task learning stress in children with ASD
findings.mechanism: A majority (7 out of 9) underscored noise as the common significant environmental factor which prompted the on-task learning effect.
findings.quote: A majority, seven out of nine participants, underscored noise as the common significant environmental factor which prompted the on-task learning effect.

findings.antecedent: Classroom environment (noise, spatial layout, lighting, colour)
findings.consequent: Effectiveness of teaching pedagogies for children with ASD
findings.mechanism: Six out of nine interviewees underscored that teaching pedagogies were affected by architectural environmental variables. Some noted a dominant teacher figure could override environmental factors.
findings.quote: Six out of nine interviewees underscored that respective teaching pedagogies for children with ASD were affected by the nature of architectural environmental variables

findings.antecedent: Classroom environment (noise, spatial layout, lighting)
findings.consequent: Children's on-task attention span and engagement level
findings.mechanism: An effective classroom model combining architectural elements with teaching pedagogies optimizes results.
findings.quote: Thematic pedagogical environment findings underlined that an effective classroom model combined architectural environment elements with teaching pedagogies to optimise results

findings.antecedent: Background noise (BN) and ambient character
findings.consequent: Impact on ASD specific classroom-learning environment
findings.mechanism: The majority of participants underlined background noise as the most significant acoustical variable, corroborated by literature review.
findings.quote: The majority of participants underlined the classroom acoustic theme, the background noise (7 out of 9 participants), as the most significant variable

mechanisms: Sensory processing dysfunctionality in children with ASD leads to stereotypical repetitive behaviours and difficulty engaging in educational tasks.
Acoustic environment (RT60, noise levels) acts as a significant environmental stressor, impacting auditory sensory processing and leading to disruptive behaviours and reduced on-task engagement.

Acoustic modification (sound-absorbent panels) reduces reverberation and noise, creating a calmer, more contained learning atmosphere, which ameliorates sensory disruptive behaviours and enhances attentiveness and on-task engagement.
The heterogeneity of ASD children means individual responses to environmental stimuli and interventions can vary.
moderators: Teacher's ability to command children's attention (Stage 1)
Spill-over impact of tantrums and meltdowns from other children (Stage 3)
implementation_implications: Cost-effective design modifications (e.g., sound-absorbent panels) can be practically implemented to address sensory noise/acoustic measures in classrooms for children with ASD.
Acoustic design guidelines based on scientific investigation are needed for learning and well-being of children with ASD.
Classroom design should provide clear visual boundaries, spaciousness, low arousal interior colour schemes, clear routes, uncluttered visuals, and quiet withdrawal spaces.
Structured teaching methodologies (e.g., TEACCH) combined with acoustically modified environments can maximize learning and minimize frustrations.
Reducing noise and visual stimuli is crucial for enhancing on-task attention and reducing disruptive behaviours in children with ASD.

limitations: Results are strictly limited to the classroom environments studied and cannot be generalized to other environmental contexts.
The small sample size (N=4) and specific ASD population group limit the generalizability of the results.
The qualitative data relied on verbal explanations and interpretations of participants' experiences, which may introduce subjectivity.
The intervention involved a fixed single mode of acoustic modification, limiting experimental flexibility to gauge graduated modification or phase shifting effects.

The study duration (six consecutive weeks) was constrained by the school calendar, which may not have been sufficient to establish participant progress stability and result verification for all heterogeneous responses.
Participant absenteeism and non-attending behaviour limited the consistency of sessions, sequence, and duration for some students.
Data was only collated for student-specific sensory disruptive and on-task behaviours, not broader impacts.
The acute heterogeneity of children with ASD led to spill-over impacts (e.g., tantrums, meltdowns) on other children, affecting the normalcy of observations.
Staff sickness or substitute teacher presence impacted participant behaviour and class-peer rapport.
